job.style: a description of a classroom activity or experiment and what it shows

response.passage: In our economics lab, we analyzed data from two fictional countries, Alpha and Beta. Alpha has a high per capita income, but wealth is concentrated in the hands of a few billionaires, leaving most citizens in poverty. Beta has a lower average income, but wealth is distributed more evenly, and the government invests heavily in public healthcare and education. We learned that development is not just about earning more money; it includes access to quality services and a better quality of life. To measure this, we looked at the Human Development Index, which considers more than just financial status. We specifically examined the literacy rate, defined as the proportion of the population aged 7 and above who can read and write with understanding in any language. A person who can only sign their name is not considered literate by this standard. Finally, we discussed how relying solely on national income metrics can be misleading. If a country increases its wealth by depleting its natural resources, it might show high growth today but face a collapse in the future. True development must be sustainable, ensuring that the progress we achieve today does not compromise the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
response.summary: Development is a multidimensional concept that goes beyond just income to include education, health, and sustainability. Relying on averages or financial metrics alone can hide inequalities and long-term risks.
